column3: Its active abandonment of the Hereafter parallels the focus's reproach for abandoning the true Creator, though the objects differ.
The command to leave deniers until their appointed day shares the abandonment verb but adds only a distant judgment context.
Allah's reference to the one He created reinforces divine creatorship and the act of leaving a matter to Him.
It condemns abandoning what the Lord created, closely paralleling the focus's charge of wrongful abandonment.
It immediately introduces Elijah's rebuke to the same people, furnishing the direct context for the focus question.
Its mention of a good reward has only a lexical connection to the focus's description of the Best Creator.
It explicitly joins Allah's excellent making with His creation of all things, supporting the focus's creator epithet.
It immediately identifies Allah as the people's Lord and Lord of their forefathers, the God abandoned for Baal.
It commands calling upon Allah under His beautiful names, directly contrasting invocation of Baal.
It concludes the stages of human formation by praising Allah as the Best of creators, repeating the focus formula.
The accusation against Moses does not clarify calling on Baal or abandoning the Creator.
It commands calling Allah by His beautiful names and abandoning those who distort them, a close corrective to the focus.
Allah's creation of humanity in the best form supports the focus's attribution of unsurpassed creative power to Him.
It immediately gives the people's rejection and consequence, completing the narrative response to Elijah's question.
Noah's plea that no disbeliever be left creates a contrary but relevant use of abandonment amid a dispute over false gods.
It praises calling people to Allah, providing a positive counterpart to calling upon Baal.
Its return to Hell belongs to the same surah but does not elucidate Elijah's indictment of Baal worship.
It affirms that Allah creates whatever He wills and possesses all dominion, directly supporting the focus's Creator contrast.
It states that those invoked besides Allah create nothing and are themselves created, directly explaining the error in invoking Baal.
The opening of Lot's rebuke does not add to the focus's issue of invocation or divine creatorship.
Paradise's good reward is only a broad lexical resonance with the focus's use of best.
Baal here means a husband, not the deity named in the focus.
The tree in Hell does not clarify the Baal-versus-Creator contrast.
Rewarding those who do good only weakly echoes the focus's use of the root for best.
Calling to the Lord's way with what is best supplies a constructive counterpart to Elijah's challenge over whom to invoke.
The command to leave Allah's she-camel concerns a distinct sign and only shares the abandonment verb.
Its statement that Hell leaves nothing is a different use of abandonment and offers only a distant judgment contrast.
Baal here means husband, not the false god challenged by Elijah.
The removal of mountains does not clarify the focus's worship and creation contrast.
The destructive wind's leaving nothing is unrelated to abandoning Allah for Baal.
Pharaoh's taunt that Moses may call his Lord supplies a hostile but relevant scene of calling upon God.
Leaving the earth level after the mountains vanish is unrelated to the focus.
The excellent reward for those who do good only broadly echoes the focus's superlative language.
Its marital use of baal and mention of creation do not concern the false deity or the focus's argument.
The description of a level plain does not add to the focus.
Leaving deniers to gradual punishment shares the verb but not the focus's false-worship contrast.
Its references to husbands are unrelated to Baal as an object of invocation.
The skeptic's question about resurrection does not clarify calling on Baal or divine creatorship.
Hell calling the one who turned away offers an inverse image of a summons whose destination exposes wrongful turning.
It declares Allah's judgment unsurpassed, a close parallel to the focus's assertion that His creative power is unsurpassed.
Leaving grain in its ears is unrelated to the focus's abandonment of the Creator.
Leaving affluent deniers to Allah's judgment shares the verb but contributes little to the Baal contrast.
Its challenge whether people created themselves directly undermines any rival claim beside Allah the Creator.
Lot's repudiation of his people's deeds does not clarify the focus.
It contrasts Allah's lordship and dominion with those invoked besides Him, who possess nothing, directly paralleling Baal worship.
The statement of Allah's punishment and mercy does not specifically illuminate invocation or creation.
The request to be left behind from striving has no material link to the focus.
The description of excellent companions in Paradise does not clarify the focus.
The condemned admitting sin adds no connection to the Baal-versus-Creator question.
It calls to Allah with insight and disavows association, a clear positive counterpart to invoking Baal.
Noah's persistent call to his people provides a prophetic counterpart to Elijah's address, though its immediate object differs.
Allah's unsurpassed coloring and exclusive worship offer only an indirect parallel to His being the Best Creator.
The episode of Joseph's appearance does not clarify the focus.
The messenger calls people to believe in their Lord, directly contrasting a call directed to Baal.
Allah's rescue of a preceding prophetic pair reinforces the surah's pattern of divine vindication, but not Elijah's specific rebuke.
Joseph resists an improper invitation, a remote ethical contrast to the focus's wrongful invocation.
The description of righteous companionship does not add to the focus.
The believers' prostration does not clarify the Baal-versus-Creator contrast.
Rescuing the righteous and leaving wrongdoers kneeling is not material to the focus's invocation.
Those formerly invoked besides Allah vanish at judgment, directly exposing the futility of invoking a rival such as Baal.
It asks whether humans create or Allah creates, directly reinforcing the focus's exclusive Creator claim.
The selection of the most rebellious for punishment does not clarify the focus.
Leaving people in their confusion shares the abandonment verb but does not illuminate whom the focus says they abandon.
Its reciprocity of goodness is only a lexical resonance with the focus's superlative description.
Joseph's stratagem and Allah's knowledge do not clarify the focus.
Calling for destruction in Hell is a different kind of invocation and only remotely contrasts the focus.
The lack of permission to speak does not clarify the focus.
The barren wind is unrelated to calling on Baal or abandoning Allah.
The contrast between expected outcomes does not add to the focus.
Past people's finer possessions do not clarify the focus's Creator epithet.
The promised day of humiliation does not clarify the focus.
It names the Lord as Creator at the outset of revelation, supporting the focus's appeal to Allah's creative authority.
Repelling evil with what is better only lexically echoes the focus's word for best.
The later year of relief in Joseph's forecast does not clarify the focus.
It commands a community to call to good, offering a general corrective model of right-directed calling.
Moses rejects seeking any deity other than Allah, directly matching Elijah's denunciation of choosing Baal instead of Allah.
Knowing who is most deserving of Hell does not elucidate the focus.
Replacing evil with good is only a lexical connection to the focus's description of the Best Creator.
It identifies Allah as creator of death and life and tests the best in deeds, supporting but not repeating the focus's creator claim.
Its military-context call for peace does not clarify invocation of a deity.
Abraham's disavowal of what his people worship besides Allah gives a close prophetic parallel to Elijah's anti-idolatry rebuke.
The polemic over alleged daughters and sons does not directly clarify the focus.
It identifies Allah as Lord, giver of form, and benefactor, strongly supporting the focus's appeal to His creative superiority.
It warns that apparent good workmanship can be misjudged, only distantly related to the focus's use of best.
Allah's true creation of the heavens, earth, and human form reinforces His exclusive creative authority.
It condemns calling a child to the Most Merciful, a direct parallel to the focus's rebuke of misdirected invocation.
Its good example repeats the prior Abrahamic theme but adds little after 60:4.
The preservation of reward for the best work has only a lexical link to the focus.
The question about Hell does not clarify the focus.
The command to abandon remaining usury shares the verb but not the focus's worship contrast.
The punishment of cursed agitators does not add to the focus.
Leaving a wife suspended is a separate legal use of the abandonment root.
Its foundational command not to associate anything with Allah directly supplies the principle violated by invoking Baal.
Abandoning the weighty Day parallels wrongful neglect but not the focus's abandonment of Allah.
Admission to mercy for righteous servants does not clarify the focus.
It contrasts following Allah's revelation with inherited custom despite a call to the Fire, relevant to entrenched idol practice.
Its detailed signs of creation offer evidence for Allah's creative power, though it does not address Baal worship.
In danger people call Allah sincerely and devote religion to Him alone, directly opposing invocation of Baal.
It challenges those who invoke alleged beings besides Allah that they cannot remove harm, directly exposing Baal's impotence.
Allah's command summons people from the earth, displaying divine authority in calling and resurrection rather than a rival invocation.
It identifies Elijah as a messenger, establishing the prophetic authority of the speaker whose rebuke culminates in the focus.
It exempts Allah's chosen servants after the rejection of Elijah, completing the immediate contrast between false worship and faithful devotion.
It condemns assigning partners to Allah despite His creating them, directly opposing the transfer of worship from the Creator to Baal.
It declares Allah the Creator of all things and commands worship of Him, directly stating the truth the focus contrasts with Baal invocation.
It challenges associating beings that create nothing and are themselves created, directly exposing the incoherence of invoking Baal.
It calls those invoked besides Allah servants like their worshippers and challenges their ability to respond, closely paralleling the focus's rebuke.
It states that those called besides Allah cannot help their worshippers or themselves, directly clarifying the futility of Baal worship.
It rejects worshipping besides Allah beings that neither harm nor benefit and calls them intercessors, directly matching the focus's polemic.
It forbids calling on besides Allah what can neither benefit nor harm, providing a direct normative counterpart to the focus question.
It asks whether powerless protectors besides Allah can be taken and contrasts divine creation with non-creation, combining both focus themes.
The messengers appeal to Allah as Creator of the heavens and earth while confronting doubt, reinforcing the Creator basis of Elijah's rebuke.
Its question whether the Creator is like one who does not create gives a concise direct rationale against elevating Baal.
It condemns worship of beings besides Allah that possess no provision or power, directly supporting the focus's rejection of Baal.
It reasons that multiple gods would corrupt the heavens and earth, supplying a foundational argument against rival divinities.
It challenges taking gods besides Allah without proof, directly framing the error at issue in the focus.
It identifies Allah as the True and what is invoked besides Him as false, directly resolving the Baal-versus-Creator contrast.
It declares that those invoked besides Allah cannot create even a fly, an especially direct counterpart to the Best of creators.
It denies any god alongside Allah and argues that rival gods would contend, directly opposing devotion to Baal.
It warns against calling on another god with no proof, directly matching the focus's denunciation of calling Baal.
It describes supposed gods besides Allah as unable to create and themselves created, directly explaining why Baal cannot rival the Creator.
It asks whether a god besides Allah created the heavens, earth, and rain-fed gardens, directly echoing the focus's Creator comparison.
Its repeated challenge, "is there a god with Allah," advances the same anti-association argument as the focus.
It asks whether any god besides Allah answers the distressed and removes harm, a direct test of the efficacy of invoked beings.
It attributes guidance and winds to Allah while repeating the challenge of a god besides Him, reinforcing exclusive divine agency.
It asks who begins creation and repeats it while providing sustenance, then challenges the claim of a god alongside Allah.
On the Day of Judgment Allah summons those whom people claimed as associates, exposing the failure of rival objects of worship.
The alleged associates are called and fail to answer, directly portraying the impotence of beings invoked besides Allah.
Its question about who created the heavens, earth, sun, and moon elicits Allah's name, reinforcing the Creator side of the focus.
It notes that people acknowledge Allah as the sender of rain and life-giver to earth, highlighting the inconsistency of their association.
It attributes creation, provision, death, and life exclusively to Allah and asks whether any associates can do any of this.
After affirming Allah's creation, it challenges others to show what those besides Him have created, directly paralleling the focus.
It commands calling the alleged beings besides Allah and states they own nothing in the heavens or earth, directly testing Baal's claimed status.
It asks whether any creator besides Allah provides from heaven and earth, directly reinforcing the focus's exclusive Creator claim.
It asks whether alleged partners created anything in the earth or share the heavens, directly dismantling the premise of invoking Baal.
It notes that people take gods besides Allah seeking help, providing a clear parallel to the misplaced reliance implied by Baal worship.
It records the admission that Allah created the heavens and earth, then challenges reliance on those called besides Him.
It rejects being commanded to worship other than Allah, directly matching Elijah's demand to abandon false worship.
It calls Allah Creator of all things and declares no god but Him, concisely joining the focus's two central claims.
It forbids worshipping those called besides Allah after clear proofs of His lordship, directly paralleling the focus.
It commands worship of Allah who created the sun and moon rather than worshipping created signs, directly supporting exclusive devotion to the Creator.
It observes that people acknowledge Allah as Creator of the heavens and earth, exposing the inconsistency behind idolatry.
It similarly records their admission that Allah created them, which sharpens the focus's challenge over abandoning Him.
It demands that those who call on beings besides Allah show what they created in the earth or their share in the heavens.
It calls most astray those who invoke besides Allah beings that cannot answer them, directly explaining the error of calling Baal.
